questions.title: How does the Tenth Circuit review BIA decisions when a single Board member affirms—what parts of the IJ’s reasoning can the court rely on?
questions.question_body: The opinion says it reviews the BIA’s decision but can consult the IJ’s 'more complete explanation' (citing Uanreroro). I’m confused about the practical scope: if the BIA issues a short affirmance focusing on a couple of grounds, can the court look to additional rationales discussed only by the IJ to uphold the result, or is it limited to the specific grounds the BIA expressly adopted? How does this interact with the substantial-evidence standard and the 'any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled' language?

questions.title: What threshold for 'past persecution' did the court apply to repeated death threats and an apparent attempted child abduction?
questions.question_body: The court emphasizes that 'threats alone' usually aren’t persecution and notes no lasting physical harm. But the record includes: (1) repeated threatening calls, (2) a death-threat brochure targeting Liberal Party 'snitches,' (3) two armed men twice confronting and threatening the family/employee, and (4) a man grabbing the child at school before the father intervened. How does the Tenth Circuit weigh the cumulative effect of armed confrontations and an apparent attempted abduction when there’s no actual injury? Are there Tenth Circuit cases where similar non-injury but highly menacing conduct did cross the persecution line?

questions.title: Why did the court find the nexus to political opinion only 'tangential' despite explicit references to the Liberal Party?
questions.question_body: Petitioners received a brochure stating 'death to snitches from Liberal Party,' and the men referenced Petitioners being 'in politics.' Yet the court concludes the 'predominant motive' was Jimenez’s interference with Don Rafa’s criminal enterprise and his supposed cooperation with the prosecutor’s office. Under the 'at least one central reason' mixed-motive standard, how did the court determine that the political-opinion motive was subordinate rather than co-equal? What evidentiary markers pushed the court toward a personal/anti-informant motive over a political one?

questions.title: What counts as showing the government is 'unable or unwilling' to protect if the applicants only spoke to individual officers and didn’t file reports?
questions.question_body: The court faults Petitioners for minimal reporting and cites attempts by authorities to search the property as evidence against government-complicity. How much reporting is required to avoid the inference that the state might have helped if asked—does informing two patrol officers suffice? What kind of proof is needed to establish that filing a formal report would have been futile or dangerous (to fit the exception), especially when there’s some evidence of police action (attempted raids) but also localized warnings by officers to 'not seek trouble'?

questions.title: Who bears the burden on internal relocation in the absence of past persecution, and how did the court weigh the short-term countryside move?
questions.question_body: Since the court found no past persecution, I understand the burden stays with Petitioners to show relocation isn’t reasonable. The panel highlights that (1) relatives remain unharmed, (2) Petitioners briefly stayed safely with Jimenez’s mother, and (3) the threats said 'leave the neighborhood' rather than the country. How do courts evaluate whether a brief three-week period in a different area is probative of long-term safety? What factors (reach of the persecutor, economic/administrative barriers, family ties, size of country) are most persuasive in the Tenth Circuit relocation analysis?

questions.title: Did Petitioners waive their 'particular social group' theory by not briefing it, and what is required to preserve a PSG claim on appeal?
questions.question_body: The opinion says Petitioners 'did not brief' arguments on a PSG and limits nexus analysis to political opinion. Is that treated as waiver/forfeiture at the circuit level due to inadequate briefing, or as failure to exhaust before the BIA? What level of specificity is required in the opening brief to preserve a PSG-based claim and its nexus theory in the Tenth Circuit?

questions.title: Does denial of asylum always foreclose withholding of removal in mixed-motive or non-state-actor cases?
questions.question_body: The court says Petitioners fail to meet the 'higher standard' for withholding because they didn’t establish a well-founded fear for asylum. I get that withholding requires a 'clear probability,' but are there scenarios where an applicant loses asylum on a discretionary or nexus ground yet still wins withholding (e.g., if one protected ground fails as 'not a central reason' but another theory could meet the withholding standard)? Or is the failure here categorical because the same factual deficiencies (no persecution, no nexus, state able to protect) defeat both forms of relief?

questions.title: What happens to derivative beneficiaries’ claims if the principal’s asylum application fails—can the spouse or children prevail independently?
questions.question_body: The children were derivative on Jimenez’s asylum application. If the principal applicant fails on past persecution/nexus/government-protection, can a derivative spouse or child still obtain asylum or withholding based on their own individualized risk (e.g., the child who was grabbed)? What procedural steps would have been needed to preserve independent claims for the family members in this posture?
